doc.title: Grover Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, February 13, 1996

title: Programming from 300 charts
summary: Mitchell balances audience favorites with challenging arrangements to keep bright musicians interested.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: When you pick from your book of arrangements, how many charts do you usually work out of?

Well we carry about 300 with us. And I try to make things flow. You know what I mean? I try to mix a certain amount of things that people want to hear and you know that it’s like standard repertoire, you know they want to hear “April in Paris” and “L’il Darling,” “One O’Clock Jump,” “Corner Pocket.” So you have to, I try to blend them into a combination of good arrangements that works within the framework of what this band is all about and at the same time to keep the musicians interested and from getting them bored. And trying to do a service too — splitting the difference between the audience and something very interesting, something swinging, and you have to keep these, these are very, very bright people and you have to keep them interested. You know how children are who are very bright in school and if you aren’t careful they lose interest? Well that’s the way these people are. You have to challenge them all the time. If you start just playing the same old easy things every night and just making the job, you’re going to get in big trouble. And you’re going to get a lot of yawning, and a lot of lack of concentration. So I’m trying to make it flow you know. I make mistakes you know. I make mistakes, it doesn’t always come off. But I’ve been lucky.
